title: Techniques for Solving Logarithmic Equations
overview: Now that you can combine logarithms, you can solve equations in which the variable is *inside* a logarithm. The method is always: isolate and combine the logarithms, rewrite in exponential form (or equate arguments), solve — and **check every root** in the original equation.
objectives: Solve simple logarithmic equations by rewriting them in exponential form
Write any number as a logarithm of a chosen base to equate arguments
Use the product, quotient and power laws to combine logarithms before solving
Solve logarithmic equations that lead to quadratic equations
Identify and reject extraneous roots, and recognise when all roots are valid
Solve problems involving sound levels and camera f-stops

lessons.title: Two key ideas
lessons.body:
Every logarithmic equation in this section is solved with one (or both) of these ideas.

**1. Rewrite in exponential form.** By definition,

$$\log_b x = y \iff b^y = x$$

So $\log(x + 4) = 1$ becomes $x + 4 = 10^1$, giving $x = 6$.

**2. Equal logarithms have equal arguments.** For the same base,

$$\log_m a = \log_m b \;\Rightarrow\; a = b$$

because a logarithmic function is one-to-one: each output comes from only one input.

Any number can be written as a logarithm, which is what makes idea 2 so useful:

$$2 = \log_5 25 = \log 100 = \log_4 16 = \log_3 9$$

So $\log_5(2x + 3) = 2$ can be written as $\log_5(2x+3) = \log_5 25$, giving $2x + 3 = 25$ and $x = 11$.

lessons.title: Simple logarithmic equations
lessons.body:
**Steps**

1. **Isolate** the logarithm (move constants, divide by a coefficient).
2. Rewrite in exponential form (or write the other side as a logarithm with the same base).
3. Solve the resulting equation.
4. **Check** that every argument in the original equation is positive.

**Example:** $4 = 2\log(p - 62)$.

$$2 = \log(p - 62) \;\Rightarrow\; p - 62 = 10^2 = 100 \;\Rightarrow\; p = 162$$

Check: $\log(162 - 62) = \log 100 = 2$, and $2\times2 = 4$ ✓.

### Graphical view
$\log(x + 4) = 1$ is the $x$-coordinate where $y = \log(x+4)$ (the graph of $\log x$ shifted 4 units left) meets the line $y = 1$.

```plot
title: log(x + 4) = 1 has root x = 6
f: log(x+4) | label=y = log(x + 4)
f: 1 | dashed; label=y = 1
domain: -4, 10
range: -2, 2
ticks: 2, 0.5
points: (6, 1)
asymptote x: -4
```

lessons.title: Combine logarithms first
lessons.body:
When an equation has several logarithms, use the **product, quotient and power laws** to combine them into a single logarithm on each side.

**Example:** $\log(x - 1) - 1 = -\log(x + 2)$.

1. Collect the logarithms: $\log(x - 1) + \log(x + 2) = 1$.
2. Product law: $\log[(x-1)(x+2)] = 1$.
3. Exponential form: $(x-1)(x+2) = 10$, so $x^2 + x - 2 = 10$.
4. Standard form: $x^2 + x - 12 = 0$, so $(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0$ and $x = -4$ or $x = 3$.
5. **Check:** $x = -4$ makes $\log(x - 1) = \log(-5)$ undefined, so reject it. $x = 3$ works.

The only solution is $x = 3$.

> Combining the logs creates the expression $\log[(x-1)(x+2)]$, which is defined in more places than the original. That is why extraneous roots appear: the original needs **each** argument positive, not just their product.

lessons.title: Checking for extraneous roots
lessons.body:
A root is **extraneous** if substituting it into the **original** equation makes any argument zero or negative.

It is **not** true that a quadratic always gives one valid and one extraneous root.

* $\log\sqrt[3]{x^2 + 48x} = \frac23$ gives $x^2 + 48x = 100$, so $x = -50$ or $x = 2$. **Both** are valid, because the only argument is $x^2 + 48x = 100 > 0$ in each case.
* $2\log(x - 1) = \log(x + 1)$ gives $(x-1)^2 = x + 1$, so $x^2 - 3x = 0$ and $x = 0$ or $x = 3$. Only $x = 3$ is valid: $x = 0$ gives $\log(-1)$.

**A quick checklist**

| For each candidate root | |
|---|---|
| Substitute into **every** argument of the **original** equation | All positive? |
| Evaluate both sides | Equal? |
| If any argument is $\le 0$ | Reject: extraneous |

lessons.title: Applications: sound, light and cameras
lessons.body:
**Loudness of sound.** In decibels, $L = 10\log\dfrac{I}{I_0}$, where $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m² is the quietest sound most people can hear.

* A concert at $I = 0.9$ W/m²: $L = 10\log\dfrac{0.9}{10^{-12}} = 10\log(9\times10^{11}) \approx 119.5$ dB.
* A 20-dB whisper: $20 = 10\log\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{I}{10^{-12}} = 10^2 \Rightarrow I = 10^{-10}$ W/m².

**Camera f-stops.** Each step of the f-stop doubles the light. The change in setting is $n = \log_2\dfrac1p$, where $p$ is the fraction of light available. On a cloudy day with $p = \frac14$: $n = \log_2 4 = 2$ stops.

> In each case the method is the same: substitute, **isolate the logarithm**, rewrite in exponential form, solve, and interpret.

keyTerms.definition: An equation in which the variable appears in the argument of a logarithm.
The form $b^y = x$ equivalent to $\log_b x = y$.
A value found while solving that makes some argument of a logarithm in the original equation zero or negative (or otherwise fails to satisfy it).
The expression inside a logarithm. In $\log(x - 4)$ it is $x - 4$, which must be positive.

misconceptions.myth: A quadratic always gives one valid and one extraneous root.
misconceptions.fact: It can give two valid roots (e.g. $\log\sqrt[3]{x^2+48x} = \frac23$), one, or none. Check each one.

misconceptions.myth: A negative root is always extraneous.
misconceptions.fact: A root is extraneous only if it makes an **argument** non-positive. $x = -50$ is valid in $\log\sqrt[3]{x^2+48x} = \frac23$.
$\log(-3)$ and $\log(-4)$ are undefined; the laws only apply to positive arguments.

misconceptions.myth: I can check a root in my simplified equation.
misconceptions.fact: Always check in the **original** equation — the simplified one may be defined where the original is not.

realWorld.title: Concert sound
realWorld.body: Sound engineers set levels in decibels. Solving $L = 10\log\frac{I}{I_0}$ for $I$ tells them the actual intensity reaching the audience — and how much hearing protection is needed.

realWorld.title: Photography
realWorld.body: Adjusting the aperture by one f-stop doubles or halves the light. Photographers solve $n = \log_2\frac1p$ to compensate for cloudy days or bright snow.

realWorld.title: The human eye
realWorld.body: Our perception of brightness is roughly logarithmic, which is why cameras and displays use logarithmic scales.

realWorld.title: Chemistry
realWorld.body: pH is a logarithmic scale; finding the hydronium ion concentration from a pH reading means rewriting a logarithmic equation in exponential form.

practice.question: Solve $\log\sqrt{x^2 + 3x} = \frac12$.
practice.solution: $x^2 + 3x = 10 \Rightarrow x = -5$ or $x = 2$. Both make $x^2 + 3x = 10 > 0$, so both are valid.

summary: Rewrite $\log_b x = y$ as $b^y = x$, or write both sides as logarithms with the same base and equate arguments.
Isolate logarithms and combine them using the product, quotient and power laws before converting.
Quadratic equations may result: solve by factoring or the quadratic formula.
Check every root in the original equation; reject any that make an argument zero or negative.
A quadratic can produce two, one or no valid roots.
Graphing both sides and finding intersections confirms the algebraic solution.

questions.text: Solve each equation and check your solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $x - {{a}} = 10^1 \Rightarrow x = {{10+a}}$. Check: $\log 10 = 1$ ✓.

(b) $x + {{c}} = 10^2 \Rightarrow x = {{100-c}}$. Check: $\log 100 = 2$ ✓.

(c) $\log(p - {{d}}) = 2 \Rightarrow p = {{100+d}}$.

questions.text: Solve $\log_{ {{b}} }({{c}}x + {{d}}) = {{k}}$. Show the step where you rewrite the equation in exponential form, and check your answer.
Solve each equation. Check each solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\log(w + 7) = -1 \Rightarrow w + 7 = 0.1 \Rightarrow w = -6.9$. Check: $w + 7 = 0.1 > 0$ ✓.

(b) $\log(k + 8) = 2 \Rightarrow k = 92$.

(c) $3\log(2n) = -6 \Rightarrow \log(2n) = -2 \Rightarrow 2n = 0.01 \Rightarrow n = 0.005$.

(d) $9 - \log_5(x + 100) = 6 \Rightarrow \log_5(x+100) = 3 \Rightarrow x + 100 = 125 \Rightarrow x = 25$.

rubric.point: (a) isolates the log and handles the negative exponent

questions.text: Solve $\log x + \log(x + {{d}}) = \log {{r*(r+d)}}$. Identify and reject any extraneous roots.
questions.modelAnswer:
Product law: $\log[x(x + {{d}})] = \log {{r*(r+d)}}$.

Equate arguments: $x^2 + {{d}}x - {{r*(r+d)}} = 0$, so $(x - {{r}})(x + {{r+d}}) = 0$.

$x = {{r}}$ or $x = -{{r+d}}$.

$x = -{{r+d}}$ makes $\log x$ undefined: reject. Check $x = {{r}}$: $\log {{r}} + \log {{r+d}} = \log {{r*(r+d)}}$ ✓.

rubric.point: Equates arguments to form a quadratic
Rejects the negative root with a reason

questions.text: Solve $\log(x - {{a}}) + \log(x + {{3-a}}) = 1$. Identify and reject any extraneous roots.
Solve $\log\sqrt[3]{x^2 + {{p}}x} = \frac23$. Check both roots for validity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Power law: $\frac13\log(x^2 + {{p}}x) = \frac23$, so $\log(x^2 + {{p}}x) = 2$ and $x^2 + {{p}}x = 100$.

$x^2 + {{p}}x - 100 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - {{r}})(x + {{100/r}}) = 0$, so $x = {{r}}$ or $x = -{{100/r}}$.

Check: for each root, $x^2 + {{p}}x = 100 > 0$, so the argument is positive and $\log\sqrt[3]{100} = \frac13(2) = \frac23$ ✓. **Both roots are valid.**

rubric.point: Writes the radical as a power and applies the power law
Checks both roots and concludes both are valid

questions.text: Solve each equation. Check for extraneous roots.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\frac12\log(x^2 + 3x) = \frac12 \Rightarrow x^2 + 3x = 10 \Rightarrow (x + 5)(x - 2) = 0$. Both $x = -5$ and $x = 2$ give $x^2 + 3x = 10 > 0$: both valid.

(b) $\frac12\log(x^2 - 48x) = 1 \Rightarrow x^2 - 48x = 100 \Rightarrow (x - 50)(x + 2) = 0$. Both $x = 50$ and $x = -2$ give $x^2 - 48x = 100 > 0$: both valid.

questions.text: Solve $\log_2(x - 4) + \log_2(x - 2) = 3$. Identify any extraneous roots.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\log_2[(x-4)(x-2)] = 3 \Rightarrow (x - 4)(x - 2) = 8$.

$x^2 - 6x + 8 = 8 \Rightarrow x^2 - 6x = 0 \Rightarrow x(x - 6) = 0$.

$x = 0$ makes $x - 4 = -4 < 0$: extraneous.

$x = 6$: $\log_2 2 + \log_2 4 = 1 + 2 = 3$ ✓.

questions.text: Solve $\log({{a}}k + {{c}}) - \log k = 1$ and check your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Quotient law: $\log\dfrac{ {{a}}k + {{c}} }{k} = 1$, so $\dfrac{ {{a}}k + {{c}} }{k} = 10$.

${{a}}k + {{c}} = 10k \Rightarrow {{10-a}}k = {{c}} \Rightarrow k = \frac{ {{c}} }{ {{10-a}} } \approx {{c/(10-a):4}}$.

Check: $k > 0$ and ${{a}}k + {{c}} > 0$, and the left side equals $\log 10 = 1$ ✓.

questions.text: Solve $\log(x + {{a}}) = 2\log(x - 1)$ algebraically. Identify any extraneous roots, and explain how a graph confirms your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Power law: $\log(x + {{a}}) = \log(x - 1)^2$, so $x + {{a}} = x^2 - 2x + 1$.

$x^2 - 3x - {{a-1}} = 0 \Rightarrow (x - {{r}})(x + {{r-3}}) = 0$, so $x = {{r}}$ or $x = -{{r-3}}$.

$x = -{{r-3}}$ makes $x - 1 < 0$, so $\log(x - 1)$ is undefined: reject.

$x = {{r}}$: left $\log {{r+a}}$, right $2\log {{r-1}} = \log {{(r-1)^2}}$ ✓.

Graph $y_1 = \log(x + {{a}})$ and $y_2 = 2\log(x - 1)$: they intersect once, at $x = {{r}}$. The graph of $y_2$ only exists for $x > 1$, so there is no intersection at the negative root.

rubric.point: Rejects the extraneous root with a reason

questions.text: Consider the statement: *\"When solving a logarithmic equation that results in a quadratic, you always obtain two roots: one valid and one extraneous.\"* Do you agree or disagree? Justify your answer with at least **two** counterexamples or supporting examples.
questions.modelAnswer:
Disagree.

* $\log\sqrt[3]{x^2 + 48x} = \frac23$ gives $x = -50$ and $x = 2$ — **both valid**.
* $\log x + \log(x+3) = 1$ gives $x = -5$ (extraneous) and $x = 2$ (valid) — one of each.
* A quadratic could also have a double root, or no real roots (e.g. $\log(x^2 + 1) = \log(x - 5)$ leads to $x^2 - x + 6 = 0$, which has none).

The number of valid roots depends on whether each root keeps every argument of the original equation positive.

rubric.point: Gives a correct example with two valid roots
Gives a second correct example (one valid, or none)
Explains the general principle for validity

questions.text: Consider $\log_4(x - 5) = 2$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that each of $\log_2 4$, $\log_4 16$, $\log_5 25$ and $\log 100$ equals the right side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which would you use to rewrite the right side, and why?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\log_2 4 = 2$, $\log_4 16 = 2$, $\log_5 25 = 2$, $\log 100 = 2$ — all equal 2.

(b) $\log_4 16$ is the most useful, because it has the same base as the left side, so the arguments can be equated: $x - 5 = 16$.

(c) $x = 21$. Check: $\log_4 16 = 2$ ✓.

questions.text: Decide whether each statement is valid. Explain your reasoning.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Not valid: $\log(-3)$ and $\log(-4)$ are undefined because logarithms of negative numbers do not exist. The product law only applies to positive arguments, so the statement has no meaning even though $(-3)(-4) = 12$.

(b) Valid: $-\log 3 - \log 4 = -(\log 3 + \log 4) = -\log 12$, and all arguments are positive.

rubric.point: (a) explains that the arguments must be positive
(b) correct justification using the product law

questions.text: Solve $\log(x + {{a}}) = 2 - \log x$. Give the solution correct to two decimal places and sketch (describe) the graphical solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\log x + \log(x + {{a}}) = 2 \Rightarrow x(x + {{a}}) = 100 \Rightarrow x^2 + {{a}}x - 100 = 0$.

$$x = \frac{-{{a}}\pm\sqrt{ {{a*a}} + 400} }{2}$$

$x \approx {{(-a+sqrt(a*a+400))/2:4}}$ or $x \approx {{(-a-sqrt(a*a+400))/2:4}}$. The negative root makes $\log x$ undefined: reject.

Graph $y_1 = \log(x + {{a}})$ and $y_2 = 2 - \log x$: one is increasing, the other decreasing, and they cross once, at $x \approx {{(-a+sqrt(a*a+400))/2:3}}$.

rubric.point: Collects logs and applies the product law

questions.text: Solve $\frac23 = \log\sqrt[3]{w^2 + 10w}$ algebraically and check for extraneous roots. Give exact answers and approximations.
questions.modelAnswer:
$\frac13\log(w^2 + 10w) = \frac23 \Rightarrow \log(w^2 + 10w) = 2 \Rightarrow w^2 + 10w - 100 = 0$.

$$w = \frac{-10\pm\sqrt{100 + 400}}{2} = -5 \pm 5\sqrt5$$

$w \approx 6.18$ or $w \approx -16.18$.

Both give $w^2 + 10w = 100 > 0$, so **both are valid**.

rubric.point: Uses the power law to remove the cube root
Exact roots by the quadratic formula

questions.text: Show that if $\log_b a = c$ and $\log_y b = c$, then $\log_a y = c^{-2}$ (for suitable positive values with $c \ne 0$).
questions.modelAnswer:
From $\log_b a = c$: $a = b^c$. From $\log_y b = c$: $b = y^c$.

Substitute: $a = (y^c)^c = y^{c^2}$.

So $y = a^{\frac{1}{c^2}}$, which in logarithmic form is $\log_a y = \frac{1}{c^2} = c^{-2}$. ∎

rubric.point: Rewrites both statements in exponential form
Substitutes to express a in terms of y
Solves for y as a power of a
Writes the result in logarithmic form

questions.text: Describe **two different methods** for checking whether a root of a logarithmic equation is extraneous. Illustrate both methods with the equation $\log_2 x + \log_2(x + 2) = 3$, whose algebra gives $x = 2$ or $x = -4$.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Method 1 — substitution:** substitute each root into every argument of the original equation. $x = -4$ gives $\log_2(-4)$, undefined: extraneous. $x = 2$: $\log_2 2 + \log_2 4 = 1 + 2 = 3$ ✓.

**Method 2 — graphing:** graph $y_1 = \log_2 x + \log_2(x+2)$ and $y_2 = 3$. $y_1$ exists only for $x > 0$, and the graphs meet only at $x = 2$, so $x = -4$ is not a solution.

(Another acceptable method: find the domain of the original equation first — here $x > 0$ — and reject any root outside it.)

rubric.point: Applies it correctly to both roots
Describes a second method (graphing or domain)

questions.text: Solve $\log_3(n^2 - 3n + 5) = 2$. Determine whether either root is extraneous, and explain why.
questions.modelAnswer:
$n^2 - 3n + 5 = 3^2 = 9 \Rightarrow n^2 - 3n - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow (n - 4)(n + 1) = 0$, so $n = 4$ or $n = -1$.

Check: $n = 4$: $16 - 12 + 5 = 9 > 0$ ✓. $n = -1$: $1 + 3 + 5 = 9 > 0$ ✓.

Neither root is extraneous: in both cases the only argument equals 9, which is positive. (The quadratic $n^2 - 3n + 5$ is actually positive for every $n$.)

rubric.point: Checks both roots in the original
